prompt: In the floating point sense, underflow is a situation in which:

options.text: The number is too small to be represented in the Exponent field
The exponent is too large to be represented in the Exponent field
The mantissa has too many digits
The sign bit is set on a positive number

explanation: Too small is underflow, too large is overflow. Both are stated against the Exponent field, which is the deck's own framing.

why.a: Correct. Too small is underflow, too large is overflow.
why.b: Wrong, that is overflow, the other half of the same sentence.
why.c: Wrong. Too many mantissa digits costs precision, not range, and the deck calls that inexact.
why.d: Wrong. The sign bit has nothing to do with either condition.

prompt: Match each condition to its definition in the deck.

pairs.right: The exponent is too large to be represented in the Exponent field
The number is too small to be represented in the Exponent field

explanation: Both definitions come from one sentence on the same slide, which is why they are so easily swapped under exam pressure.

prompt: Arithmetic underflow can occur when the true result of a floating point operation is:

options.text: Smaller in magnitude, that is closer to zero, than the smallest value representable as a normal floating point number in the target datatype
Larger in magnitude than the largest representable value

explanation: Closer to zero than the smallest normal value. The words closer to zero matter, because a very large negative number is not an underflow.

why.a: Correct, and the deck spells out that smaller in magnitude means closer to zero.
why.b: Wrong, that is overflow.
why.c: Wrong. Zero is representable exactly.
why.d: Wrong. Sign is irrelevant; magnitude is what matters.

prompt: Arithmetic underflow occurs when the true result is smaller in magnitude than the smallest value representable as a {{1}} floating point number in the target datatype.
explanation: Normal. The word is doing real work: values below the smallest normal number are not all lost at once, but they are no longer normal floating point numbers.

prompt: If the exponent part can represent values from minus 127 to 127, a result with a value less than which figure may cause underflow?
explanation: Less than minus 127. Underflow can in part be regarded as negative overflow of the exponent, so it is the bottom of the exponent range that is breached.

why.a: Correct, and the figure is the bottom of the stated exponent range.
why.b: Wrong. Exceeding plus 127 is overflow.
why.c: Wrong. An exponent of 0 is perfectly ordinary.
why.d: Wrong. Minus 1023 is the double precision bias, not the single precision exponent limit.

prompt: Underflow can in part be regarded as {{1}} overflow of the exponent of the floating point value.
explanation: Negative overflow. It is a useful way to hold the pair: both conditions are the exponent running off an end of its range, just different ends.

prompt: To reduce the chances of underflow or overflow, the deck says you can use:
explanation: 64-bit double precision. Its 11-bit exponent reaches about 10 to the power plus or minus 308, against single precision's 38.

why.a: Correct. 64-bit double precision.
why.b: Wrong. Single precision is the narrower option, so it makes the problem more likely, not less.
why.c: Wrong, and a 16-bit signed integer is precisely what destroyed the Ariane 5 on the next slide.
why.d: Wrong. BCD is a decimal digit code, not a floating point format.

prompt: To reduce the chances of underflow or overflow, use {{1}}-bit double-precision arithmetic.
explanation: 64 bits. The deck then shows two cases of what happens when arithmetic goes wrong: the Ariane 5 and the Vancouver Stock Exchange.

prompt: How long after lift-off did the unmanned Ariane 5 rocket explode?
explanation: Just forty seconds after lift-off, on 4 June 1996, on its first voyage, after a decade of development costing 7 billion dollars.

why.a: Correct. Just forty seconds after lift-off, on 4 June 1996, on its first voyage, after a decade of development costing 7 billion dollars.
why.b: Wrong. The deck says forty seconds.
why.c: Wrong unit. Just forty seconds after lift-off, on 4 June 1996, on its first voyage, after a decade of development costing 7 billion dollars.
why.d: Wrong on both count and unit.

prompt: On June 4, {{1}} an unmanned Ariane 5 rocket launched by the European Space Agency exploded, after a decade of development costing {{2}} billion dollars.
explanation: 1996, and 7 billion dollars. 1982 is the other date in this section, and it belongs to the Vancouver Stock Exchange.

topic: what went wrong on the Ariane 5
prompt: What was the software error that destroyed the Ariane 5?

options.text: A 64 bit floating point number was converted to a 16 bit signed integer, and the value was too large for it
A 16 bit integer was converted to a 64 bit floating point number
A value was truncated rather than rounded

explanation: A 64 bit floating point number relating to the horizontal velocity of the rocket with respect to the platform was converted to a 16 bit signed integer, and the conversion failed. Note that the slide gives the limit as 32678; the largest 16-bit signed integer is in fact 32767.

why.a: Correct, and it is an overflow on conversion, not in the arithmetic itself.
why.b: Wrong direction. Widening a value is safe; it was the narrowing that failed.
why.c: Wrong. Truncation rather than rounding is the Vancouver Stock Exchange case on the next slide.
why.d: Wrong. The value was too large, not too close to zero.

topic: what went wrong on the Ariane 5
prompt: The 64 bit floating point number that failed to convert related to the {{1}} velocity of the rocket with respect to the platform.
explanation: Horizontal velocity. The Ariane 5 flew a different trajectory from its predecessor, so a value that had always been small on the old rocket was not small on the new one.

prompt: The Vancouver stock exchange index was instituted in 1982 at a value of 1000.000. What had it fallen to twenty two months later?
explanation: It had fallen to 520, while the correctly rounded calculation gave 1098.892. The index had lost almost half its value to arithmetic alone.

why.a: Correct. It had fallen to 520, while the correctly rounded calculation gave 1098.
why.b: Wrong. 1098.892 is what the rounded calculation gave, that is the value it should have shown.
why.c: Wrong. The deck says 520.
why.d: Wrong. That figure appears nowhere.

prompt: In {{1}} the Vancouver stock exchange instituted a new index initialized to a value of {{2}}, updated after each transaction.
explanation: 1982, starting at 1000.000. Updating after each transaction is what let a tiny error per update compound into a huge one.

prompt: What caused the Vancouver index to drift so far from its true value?

options.text: The updated value was truncated rather than rounded
The updated value was rounded rather than truncated
A 64 bit float was narrowed to a 16 bit integer

explanation: Truncated rather than rounded. Truncation always loses in the same direction, so thousands of updates pushed the index steadily down.

why.a: Correct, and the direction of the bias is why the error only ever grew.
why.b: Wrong, and reversed: rounding is what should have been done, and it gave 1098.892.
why.c: Wrong. That is the Ariane 5.
why.d: Wrong. No exponent condition is involved.

prompt: The correctly rounded calculation gave the Vancouver index a value of {{1}}.
explanation: 1098.892 against the 520 actually displayed, a gap of well over five hundred points from a difference in rounding alone.

prompt: In the deck's example, 976,000,000,000,000 is written in scientific notation as:
explanation: 9.76 times 10 to the power 14. Its companion on the slide is 0.0000000000000976, which is 9.76 times 10 to the power minus 14.

why.a: Correct. 9. 9.76 times 10 to the power 14. Its companion on the slide is 0.0000000000000976, which is 9.76 times 10 to the power minus 14.
why.b: Wrong by one in the exponent.
why.c: Wrong sign, and that is the small companion value.
why.d: Wrong form. Scientific notation puts a single digit before the point.

prompt: The deck writes 0.0000000000000976 as 9.76 times 10 to the power {{1}}.
explanation: Minus 14. The pair of examples makes the point that one notation covers both the very large and the very small.

prompt: A number represented by M times B to the power plus or minus E is stored in a binary word with which fields?
explanation: The base B is implicit and need not be stored, which is why it costs no bits. The sign, exponent and mantissa are the three that do.

why.a: Correct, the mantissa is stored.
why.b: Correct, the exponent E is stored.
why.c: Correct, and it is the one bit at the front of both single and double precision.
why.d: Wrong. The deck says the base B is implicit and need not be stored.

prompt: In the form M times B to the power plus or minus E, the base B is {{1}} and need not be stored.
explanation: Implicit. Every number in the format shares the same base, so recording it in each one would be a waste of bits.

prompt: Which standards does the deck name for representing floating point?
explanation: IEEE-754, 854. The second number is easy to miss, since 754 is the one usually quoted.

why.a: Correct, both are on the slide.
why.b: Wrong, incomplete: 854 is named alongside it.
why.c: Wrong. ISO 8859-1 is the extended ASCII table.
why.d: Wrong. Not mentioned in this course.

prompt: It is called floating point because the decimal point can {{1}}.
explanation: Move. The exponent says where the point sits, so the same bits can express a huge number or a tiny fraction.

prompt: Single precision floating point can represent numbers of roughly what order?

options.text: 10 to the power plus or minus 38
10 to the power plus or minus 308
10 to the power plus or minus 127
10 to the power plus or minus 23

explanation: About 10 to the power plus or minus 38 for single precision, against 10 to the power plus or minus 308 for double.

why.a: Correct. About 10 to the power plus or minus 38 for single precision, against 10 to the power plus or minus 308 for double.
why.b: Wrong. That is double precision.
why.c: Wrong. 127 is the single precision exponent bias, not the decimal range.
why.d: Wrong. 23 is the number of mantissa bits in single precision.

prompt: Floating point is useful for scientific calculations. What can it represent?
explanation: Both ends of the scale, which is the whole reason for the format.

why.a: Correct, very large integers is the first item.
why.b: Correct, very small fractions is the second.
why.c: Wrong. Character strings need an alphanumeric code such as ASCII.
why.d: Wrong. Addresses are integers and are not stored in floating point.

prompt: How is a 32-bit single precision floating point number laid out?

options.text: 1 sign bit, an 8-bit excess-127 exponent, and a 23-bit mantissa fraction
1 sign bit, a 23-bit exponent, and an 8-bit mantissa fraction
1 sign bit, an 11-bit exponent, and a 20-bit mantissa fraction
8 sign bits, a 1-bit exponent, and a 23-bit mantissa

explanation: 1 plus 8 plus 23 is 32. The exponent is stored in excess-127 form, which is what the bias of 127 means.

why.a: Correct. 1 plus 8 plus 23 is 32.
why.b: Wrong, the two field widths are swapped.
why.c: Wrong. 11 exponent bits belong to double precision.
why.d: Wrong. There is exactly one sign bit.

prompt: Single precision is {{1}} bits in total, with a {{2}}-bit mantissa fraction.
explanation: 32 bits, of which 23 are the mantissa fraction. Add the 8-bit exponent and the 1 sign bit and the 32 is accounted for.

prompt: The value represented by a single precision number is:

options.text: plus or minus 1.M times 2 to the power E prime minus 127
plus or minus M times 2 to the power E prime minus 127
plus or minus 1.M times 2 to the power E prime minus 1023
plus or minus 1.M times 10 to the power E prime minus 127

explanation: The leading 1 is implied, the stored exponent has 127 subtracted from it, and the base is 2.

why.a: Correct. The leading 1 is implied, the stored exponent has 127 subtracted from it, and the base is 2.
why.b: Wrong. The 1 in front of the point is implicit and must be restored.
why.c: Wrong bias. 1023 belongs to double precision.
why.d: Wrong base. The base is 2, not 10.

prompt: In single precision, a sign bit of 0 signifies:
explanation: 0 is plus and 1 is minus, the same convention as sign magnitude for integers.

why.a: Correct. 0 is plus and 1 is minus, the same convention as sign magnitude for integers.
why.b: Wrong, that is a sign bit of 1.
why.c: Wrong. Zero is signalled by the whole pattern, not by the sign bit alone.
why.d: Wrong. Underflow is an exponent condition.

prompt: How is a double precision floating point number laid out?

options.text: 64 bits: 1 sign bit, an 11-bit excess-1023 exponent, and a 52-bit mantissa fraction
64 bits: 1 sign bit, an 8-bit excess-127 exponent, and a 55-bit mantissa fraction
32 bits: 1 sign bit, an 11-bit exponent, and a 20-bit mantissa fraction
64 bits: 2 sign bits, a 10-bit exponent, and a 52-bit mantissa fraction

explanation: 1 plus 11 plus 52 is 64, and the exponent is stored in excess-1023 form.

why.a: Correct. 1 plus 11 plus 52 is 64, and the exponent is stored in excess-1023 form.
why.b: Wrong. 8 bits and a bias of 127 are single precision figures.
why.c: Wrong total. Double precision is 64 bits.
why.d: Wrong. There is one sign bit, and the exponent is 11 bits.

prompt: Double precision uses an {{1}}-bit excess-1023 exponent and a {{2}}-bit mantissa fraction, and can represent numbers of the order of 10 to the power plus or minus 308.
explanation: 11 and 52. Set them against single precision's 8 and 23 and the whole comparison is in hand.

prompt: The value represented by a double precision number is plus or minus 1.M times 2 to the power:
explanation: Minus 1023, the double precision bias. The single precision formula is the same shape with 127 in its place.

why.a: Correct. Minus 1023, the double precision bias.
why.b: Wrong, that is the single precision bias.
why.c: Wrong. 308 is the decimal order of magnitude, not the bias.
why.d: Wrong sign. The bias is subtracted from the stored exponent.

prompt: Match each figure to the precision it belongs to.
explanation: Eight figures, four a side. Every one of them has been asked about on a past paper, so this mapping is worth being fluent in.

prompt: Select the operations the IEEE Standard requires at a minimum.
explanation: Seven required operations. Remainder and square root are the two most often forgotten, and logarithm is not among them.

why.a: Correct, add heads the list.
why.b: Correct, subtract is second.
why.c: Correct, multiply is third.
why.d: Correct, divide is fourth.
why.e: Correct, remainder is fifth and easily missed.
why.f: Correct, square root is sixth and is a genuine surprise on a minimum list.
why.g: Correct, decimal and binary conversion closes the list.
why.h: Wrong. Logarithm is not required by the standard as the deck presents it.

prompt: The IEEE Standard requires {{1}} operations at a minimum.

blanks.hint: add, subtract, multiply, divide, remainder, square root, decimal and binary conversion

explanation: Seven. Counting only the four familiar arithmetic operations is the usual undercount.

prompt: Select the IEEE floating point exceptions the deck lists.
explanation: Five exceptions: underflow, overflow, divide by 0, inexact, invalid. Truncation is what went wrong in Vancouver, but it is not an IEEE exception.

why.a: Correct, underflow is first.
why.b: Correct, overflow is second.
why.c: Correct, divide by 0 is third.
why.d: Correct, inexact is fourth and is the one raised by ordinary rounding.
why.f: Wrong. Truncated is not one of the five, although the Vancouver case shows how much damage truncation can do.

prompt: Besides underflow, overflow, divide by 0 and invalid, the fifth IEEE exception is {{1}}.
explanation: Inexact. It fires whenever a result has to be rounded, which for a value like 0.2 in binary is almost always.

prompt: In step 1 of putting 64.2 into IEEE single precision, what is 64 in binary?
explanation: 64 is 2 to the power 6, so it is a 1 followed by six zeros: 1000000.

why.a: Correct, seven digits in all.
why.b: Wrong. That is 32.
why.c: Wrong. That is 128.
why.d: Wrong. That is 65.

prompt: The fractional part .2 is found by repeated doubling, and gives the repeating pattern {{1}}.
explanation: 0011, repeating for ever. That is why 0.2 can never be stored exactly in binary, however many bits you use.

prompt: In the repeated doubling for .2, the third step is .8 times 2, which is 1.6. What digit does it contribute?
explanation: The digit is the whole part of the product, so 1.6 contributes 1 and leaves .6 to carry forward. The four steps give 0, 0, 1, 1, and then the pattern repeats.

why.a: Correct, the whole part of 1.6.
why.b: Wrong. 0 is contributed when the product is less than 1, as in the first two steps.
why.c: Wrong. The 6 is the fractional part carried into the next step, not the digit emitted.
why.d: Wrong. 8 is the input to this step, not its output.

prompt: Putting the halves back together, 64.2 in binary is {{1}}.0011001100110011 and on.
explanation: 1000000.0011001100110011 and on. The whole part terminates; the fraction never does.

prompt: Normalising 1000000.00110011 and on gives 1.00000000110011 and on, times 2 to the power:
explanation: The point moves six places left, so the true exponent is 6. 133 is what it becomes after the bias is added, and 127 is the bias itself.

why.a: Correct, and the deck calls 6 the true exponent.
why.b: Wrong by one. Count the places the point moves, not the digits before it.
why.c: Wrong. 133 is the biased exponent, 6 plus 127.
why.d: Wrong. 127 is the bias.

prompt: Step 2 is to {{1}} the binary representation, that is, make it look like scientific notation.
explanation: Normalize. The result always has exactly one 1 before the point, which is why that 1 can then be left implicit.

prompt: With a true exponent of 6, what is the biased exponent stored for E, in binary?
explanation: 6 plus 127 is 133, and 133 in 8-bit unsigned is 1000 0101.

why.a: Correct. 6 plus 127 is 133, and 133 in 8-bit unsigned is 1000 0101.
why.b: Wrong. That is 6 itself, with no bias added.
why.c: Wrong. That is 127, the bias alone.
why.d: Wrong. That is 134, one too many.

prompt: For the standard form the exponent needs to be in biased-127 form, so 6 plus 127 is {{1}}, whose 8-bit unsigned representation is {{2}}.
explanation: 133, which is 10000101. Adding the bias is what lets a signed exponent be stored in an unsigned field.

prompt: The mantissa stored, F, is taken from where in the normalised form, and how much of it?

options.text: The 23 bits to the right of the radix point
The 23 bits to the left of the radix point
The 8 bits to the right of the radix point

explanation: 23 bits, all of them to the right of the point. The single 1 to the left is implicit and is not stored.

why.a: Correct. 23 bits, all of them to the right of the point.
why.b: Wrong. After normalising there is only one digit to the left of the point.
why.c: Wrong. 32 is the whole word, which also holds the sign and the exponent.
why.d: Wrong. 8 is the exponent width.

prompt: Step 4 of the worked example also requires including the correct sign bit.
explanation: It does. For 64.2 the sign bit is 0, since the number is positive, and the finished pattern begins with that 0.

why.true: Correct. The deck says put it all together and include the correct sign bit.
why.false: Wrong. The sign bit is part of the assembly step and is stated on the slide.

prompt: In the finished single precision representation of 64.2, what are S and E?
explanation: S is 0 because 64.2 is positive, and E is 10000101, which is the biased exponent 133.

why.a: Correct. S is 0 because 64.
why.b: Wrong. A sign bit of 1 would make the number negative.
why.c: Wrong. 01111111 is 127, the bias, not the biased exponent.
why.d: Wrong. 00000110 is the true exponent 6, before the bias is added.

prompt: The stored mantissa F for 64.2 is {{1}}.
explanation: 00000000110011001100110, twenty three bits. The repeating 0011 pattern is simply cut off when the field runs out, which is where the inexactness comes from.

prompt: What is the IEEE single precision representation of 64.2 in hexadecimal?

why.a: Correct. The 32 bits group into 0100 0010 1000 0000 0110 0110 0110 0110, which is 42806666h.
why.b: Wrong. Check the third byte: the repeating pattern gives 66, not 06.
why.c: Wrong. BE7BAC10h is the value set in Quiz 3, a different number.
why.d: Wrong. The second hex digit comes from the exponent and is 2, not 0.

prompt: Grouped into fours, the representation of 64.2 begins {{1}} 0010 1000 0000 and ends in the repeating hexadecimal digits {{2}}.
explanation: 0100 at the front, and 6666 at the back. The repeating 6 in hexadecimal is the repeating 0110 in binary, which is the tail of the endless 0011 pattern of 0.2.

prompt: Select the values the exercise slide asks students to represent in IEEE format.

options.text: 9.999 times 10 to the 1, plus 1.610 times 10 to the minus 1
1.10 times 10 to the 10, times 9.2 times 10 to the minus 5

explanation: Four exercise items. 64.2 is the worked example the exercise follows, not one of the questions set.

why.a: Correct, 10.5 is the first exercise.
why.b: Correct, and it asks for an addition before the conversion.
why.c: Correct, and it asks for a multiplication first.
why.d: Correct, another multiplication.
why.e: Wrong. 64.2 is the worked example immediately above the exercise.

prompt: Quiz 3 asks for the decimal value of which hexadecimal number, represented in IEEE single precision format?
explanation: BE7BAC10h. Its leading hex digit B is 1011 in binary, so the sign bit is 1 and the value is negative.

why.a: Correct. BE7BAC10h.
why.b: Wrong. 42806666h is the answer to the worked example, 64.2.
why.c: Wrong. A34E is from the hexadecimal conversion section.
why.d: Wrong. FF4A is minus 182 from the revision telemetry question.

prompt: Quiz 3 also asks students to represent minus 82 using sign-magnitude, 1's and 2's complement.
explanation: It does. The quiz has two questions and they cross both topics: one floating point, one signed integers.

why.true: Correct. Minus 82 in all three integer schemes is the second question.
why.false: Wrong. The second question on the quiz slide asks for exactly that.
